newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Canada offers British Tories glimpse of poll nightmare.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Canada offers British Tories glimpse of poll nightmare.

text.p: If poor opinion poll showings are not enough to dishearten British Conservatives before Thursday's election, then surveying the disaster that befell their Canadian counterparts almost certainly will be.

While a Canadian-style drubbing is unlikely for the Conservative Party, political analysts note a number of similarities to the 1993 Canadian election -- not least the overwhelming craving for change among a jaded electorate.

"I've thought for some time there was no way back for the Conservatives here and I think that's partly a response to my Canadian experience," said Peter Clarke, professor of modern British history at Cambridge University.
"A government that has been long discredited in the eyes of the voters has not been able to pull back the sort of ground required."

Clarke, who keeps a home in Vancouver, was there in October 1993 when the Canadian Conservatives were sent packing to the political wilderness. Their majority was reduced to a mere two out of 295 parliamentary seats.

The monumental scale of defeat was a surprise -- even media darling prime minister Kim Campbell lost her seat just after succeeding Brian Mulroney as leader -- but a rejection of the Conservative government after nine years in power was not.
The list of voters' laments was long: rising taxes, including a new value-added tax, ballooning deficits, the inability to smooth relations with Quebec.
But most critically, voters were fed up with the air of sleaze, patronage and arrogance that clung to the Mulroney government and wanted something, and someone, new.
SIMILAR FRUSTRATIONS AND SIMILAR PATTERNS
After 18 years of Conservative rule, analysts detect the same frustration among British voters.

Although Prime Minister John Major's personal reputation has remained untarnished, "sleaze" has become a major focus of the British campaign amid allegations that Conservative former minister Neil Hamilton accepted cash to ask parliamentary questions.
Scandals became so rife that Major appointed a committee to lay down better guidelines for legislators.
"Neil Hamilton is the abiding symbol of the pattern of petty corruption that has persistently dogged the government of John Major," Clarke said.
But Major's party should manage more than two seats. Its power base is spread out much more evenly across the country.

"Clearly what went wrong in Canada for the Tories, apart from a very bad campaign, was they lost their regional support areas -- Quebec and the west," said Jed Martin, director of Canadian studies at the University of Edinburgh.
"That kind of regional disaster is not going to hit the Tories." Even if the Conservatives lost badly, they would still retain around 150 seats in the 659-seat parliament, he said.
Another striking similarity between the two countries has been the big swing to the centre by left-leaning parties, which some analysts see as a western phenomenon.

Since getting into power, the Canadian Liberal Party under Prime Minister Jean Chretien, has slashed the deficit, cut interest rates to 40-year lows, and brought about an economic recovery remarkably devoid of inflation.

"They are ridding themselves of the historic tax and spend image going back to the (Pierre) Trudeau era and that is broadly similar to what New Labour is coming up with here," Clarke said of Tony Blair's transformed opposition Labour Party.

So radical has been the change that analysts can barely find a difference between the economic policies of the British Conservatives and Labour. Blair has promised low inflation, tough spending controls and no income tax rises.

That is why financial markets in Britain so far have been unusually serene about the prospect of a Labour government, said Jonathan Elkins, a Canadian bond dealer at Levesque Beaubien Geoffrion in London.
He identified a similar situation in the United States.
"The Democrats adopted very Republican-esque policies as demanded by the electorate," he said. An agreement by President Bill Clinton to work towards a balanced budget was one example.
Martin said financial markets and economic integration have prompted this move.

"We assumed 20 years ago that governments control the destiny of countries. With globalisation -- particlarly those expressed in economic blocs like the European Union or NAFTA (the North American Free Trade Agreement) -- that limits the degree of freedom that governments have," he said.
